text: This report is based on information available at the time of publication. Mayor and City Councilmembers, I am pleased to present the 2025 Mid-Year City Council Priority Progress Report. This is a brief update on the progress made to address the priorities you set forth during the City Council Retreat in February of 2025. Priorities for 2025 center on (1) economic development and financial sustainability, (2) public safety, (3) environmental sustainability, and (4) homelessness response. The achievements noted in this report would not have been possible without the hard work of our dedicated City staff. As we enter the second half of 2025, the City of Fremont remains committed to focusing existing resources in support of the City Council’s policy interests, maintaining the current level of programs and services, while ensuring a balanced Operating Budget. Some of the progress that the City has made during the first half of 2025 includes, but is not limited to, the opening of new affordable housing developments, citywide transition towards renewable energy, enhancement of emergency preparedness, and surging levels of business and real estate investment in Fremont. This report is intended to share a sample of our progress at the mid-year point, and we will provide a more comprehensive report at the end of this year. Thank you for your unwavering commitment to the City of Fremont, and I look forward to continuing our collaborative effort to serve our communities. Sincerely, Karena Shackelford City Manager

✓ Adopted a balanced Fiscal Year 2025/26 Operating Budget, which maintains essential services prioritized by the City Council. ✓ To ensure the City’s fiscal sustainability and account for looming uncertainty in economic conditions, the adopted Operating Budget suspends $3.2 million in transfers from the general fund for pavement and median maintenance, tree trimming, and park capital replacement to help balance this year’s budget. ✓ The adopted Operating Budget includes service enhancements to include supporting wildfire prevention activities, customer service at the Animal Shelter, rental assistance for homeless prevention, temporary shelter for homeless individuals, and additional homeless encampment cleanup services. ✓ Adopted a new 5-year Capital Improvement Plan, allocating funding to important infrastructure investments in our community, including traffic/transportation enhancements, public facility/road maintenance, continued funding for the new Central Park Community Center, and various other park improvements. ✓ Attracted numerous new retail businesses to Fremont, including two Michelin-listed eateries and several new downtown retailers. ✓ Facilitated the development of major new industrial campuses, including the full lease-up of Fremont Technology Center, the groundbreaking of Campus at Bayside, the application submittal for Sobrato’s Tech Campus, and the application submittal of Prologis Bayside. Ultimately, these projects are expected to provide over $20 million in revenue via one-time impact fees and recurring property tax and sales and business tax from new businesses. ✓ Supported major expansions of electric grid infrastructure to support continued advanced industry growth, grid resilience, and infill redevelopment in Fremont. This includes two new 75 megavoltamperes transformers in Bayside and Warm Springs, an 18-megawatt Bloom Energy microgrid, and one gigawatt of regional capacity through LS Power’s “Power the Bay” project. Collectively, these projects represent a more than $500 million investment in electrical capacity in Fremont. ✓ Held multiple industry and community events, including The Registry Bus Tour, Silicon Valley Commercial Real Estate Outlook, Engineering Expo, and Future of Fremont, all aimed at bringing key business stakeholders into Fremont and better telling our story. ✓ Expanded Fremont’s leading cluster of AI hardware manufacturers to include seven of the ten largest companies globally. These businesses contribute significantly to Fremont’s economy.

✓ Added a new fire company to better serve the community, comprised of a new fire truck, T56, and nine firefighters, three per shift. This additional apparatus is strategically housed at the Central Avenue fire station, positioned to provide swift and reliable protection to its surrounding areas. ✓ Restarted the Fremont Fire Department’s (FFD) Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) program, empowering residents to play an active role in disaster response. ✓ Began assessing fire safety by inspecting fire hydrants and working with the Alameda County Water District to address issues with the goal of making sure every hydrant in Fremont gets inspected annually to ensure proper working order when a disaster strikes. ✓ Upgraded to Phoenix G2 Station Alerting System to better streamline communication and improve FFD response times. Fremont is the first city in the county to use this cutting-edge technology, providing better notifications, which should result in faster and more effective service delivery to the community. ✓ The Fremont Police Department (FPD) developed a new Strategic Plan, shaped by community feedback, outlining goals through 2027. ✓ In January, the FPD became the first police agency in California certified by the International Association of Chiefs of Police Trust Building Campaign, having met 25 key policies and best practices that strengthen relationships and foster collaboration. ✓ Since January, the FPD has hired 23 well-qualified police officers, thanks to additional recruiting and retention strategies, such as including a substantial hiring bonus. This effort has helped the FPD bring its overall number of police officer vacancies down to 27 as of June 25, 2025, reducing the number of vacancies by over 32% since January. ✓ Partnered with Joshua’s Gift, a nonprofit foundation, to launch Code Joshua in April, one of the first autism registries of its kind in the region. ✓ Partnered with California School for the Deaf to better understand the needs of this community. Also, began training programs for police officers on responding to persons with dementia. ✓ Added two new highly trained bomb detection dogs, K-9 Nala, who has already proven invaluable in keeping Fremont safe, and more recently, K-9 Rusty. ✓ The City Council approved over $700,000 in grant funding for use by the FPD to purchase front-line equipment, including additional drones, crime mitigation technology, and safety equipment. In direct support of crime reduction and safety objectives, the City Council has also approved over $800,000 of a $2.5 million grant to initiate the build-out of the FPD’s state-of-the-art Real Time Information Center (RTIC). Additionally, the FPD utilized approximately $75,000 from a traffic safety grant to conduct special traffic safety enforcement missions. ✓ The FPD and FFD enhanced emergency preparedness by completing Incident Command System (ICS) training, conducting incident debriefs, purchasing relevant equipment, and assessing overall needs, preparation, and readiness.

✓ Received an “A” grade from the Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP) and eight out of nine Global Covenant for Mayors badges for the City’s climate action efforts. ✓ High-profile utility infrastructure investments are underway, including the $500 million “Power the Bay” project, connecting nearly one gigawatt from Central Valley solar farms to Fremont’s Bayside transmission station and a 115-megawatt local grid expansion to support expanded manufacturing in Fremont. This project will also provide five miles of dedicated fiberoptic broadband conduit to the City for future use. ✓ Facilitated major grid infrastructure expansions with the California Independent System Operator (CAISO), Pacific Gas and Electric Company (PG&E), and other stakeholders to position Fremont for sustainable growth and development for decades to come. ✓ The City is electrifying its buildings and fleet by upgrading to advanced heat pump technologies, purchasing electric vehicles to replace the aging gas-powered fleet, and installing charging infrastructure. ✓ City staff and community partners continue to plant thousands of trees throughout Fremont as part of the City’s implementation of its Urban Forest Management Plan. ✓ The City Council approved Fremont’s first-ever Active Transportation Plan, which focuses on walkability and safe mobility. ✓ Began Fremont’s transition to 100% renewable energy, while maintaining affordable choices. Fremont residents will transition to Ava Community Energy’s Renewable 100 service plan in August, or they can opt for another plan.

✓ Added First United Methodist Church as a sixth site to the Safe Parking Program to increase capacity. The program assisted 26 residents in Fiscal Year 24/25. ✓ Supported Abode Services’ Sunrise Village Shelter to fill a Fiscal Year 24/25 operating budget gap and maintain shelter bed capacity. ✓ Achieved our highest success rate to date for the Winter Relief Program, transitioning 46% of participants into housing, shelter, or the Safe Parking Program. ✓ Received City Council approval for a new contract to operate the Housing Navigation Center (HNC) for an additional two years, with possible extensions based on funding availability. In all, 279 people have been served since the HNC opened in 2020. Sixty percent of people who left the program went into stable housing. ✓ Expanded encampment cleanups across the city from 2.5 days a week to three. ✓ Passed a new camping ordinance to discourage long-term, public encampments in Fremont. ✓ Hired a new outreach case manager and mental health clinician to support the City’s Mobile Evaluation Team and homeless street outreach efforts. ✓ Held a stakeholder workshop in partnership with Urban Land Institute (ULI) to generate new ideas and partnerships to expand Winter Relief and non-congregate shelters throughout Fremont. The report from the workshop was published by ULI. ✓ Helped celebrate the new Fremont Family Apartments, a 54-unit affordable housing project. In 2025 alone, the City will open five new affordable housing developments, providing 567 new affordable housing units for low-income households. ✓ Engaged in promoting transit-oriented development and streamlining approvals for accessory dwelling units (ADUs). The City launched pre-approved ADU plans, enabling an expedited review timeline and lower permitting costs.
